title: Failure Classes, Data Paths & Command-Response Diagnosis

content.overview: Automated-system faults can arise from sensor quality, communications, configuration, controller logic, equipment non-response, distribution or insufficient capacity. Specialists classify the failure domain from evidence before naming an internal root cause.

vocabulary.definition: Failure in sensing, communication, logging or display that prevents trustworthy process information.
A commanded output that does not produce the expected physical equipment state or process change.
A condition where functioning equipment cannot keep up with the actual process load.

sections.title: Separate sensor, control and equipment layers
sections.body: A bad sensor can trigger the wrong command, a correct command can fail to reach equipment, and running equipment can still fail to achieve the crop-zone condition. Test each layer.

sections.title: Use independent corroboration
sections.body: Compare controller logs with equipment state, neighboring/verified sensors and crop-zone outcome before deciding which layer failed.

sections.title: Preserve contradictions
sections.body: Conflicting data are diagnostic evidence. Do not delete one source simply because another source is more convenient.

workedExamples: A controller shows cooling ON, the unit is physically running, but canopy temperature continues rising; the evidence points away from a pure command failure and toward distribution/capacity or measurement issues.
commonMistakes: Calling every fault a controller problem.
Trusting display status without physical verification.
Changing several configuration values before classifying the fault.
content.practicalApplication: Classify six mock failures into sensor/data path, command/configuration, equipment response, distribution, capacity or unresolved.
content.summary: Reliability diagnosis works by separating failure layers and testing them independently.
